1→//! Implementation of [Beacon Chain Fork Choice].
     2→//!
     3→//! Time is scarce and writing is hard, so the documentation is rather fragmented.
     4→//! `fork_choice_control::extra_tests` has some diagrams that may help.
     5→//!
     6→//! We group unfinalized blocks into segments, each of which corresponds to a fork and contains
     7→//! blocks starting from the point when the fork first appeared and ending with the tip of the fork.
     8→//!
     9→//! A chain may consist of multiple segments, with each segment branching off the previous one. In
    10→//! the ideal case the whole chain will be contained in a single segment. This should almost always
    11→//! be the case when syncing old blocks.
    12→//!
    13→//! Segments are assigned sequential IDs.
    14→//! The IDs do not correspond to anything outside the application.
    15→//!
    16→//! Segments are kept in a map ordered by their IDs.
    17→//! This has the effect of keeping unfinalized blocks topologically ordered.
    18→//!
    19→//! Segments are not uniquely represented. A chain with forks may be divided into segments in
    20→//! multiple ways, depending on what order its blocks are received in.
    21→//!
    22→//! We assume finalized parts of the chain cannot be forked.
    23→//! Finalized blocks are moved into a contiguous vector.
    24→//!
    25→//! We assume that the number of forks will be low. Some algorithms used here slow down linearly as
    26→//! the number of forks increases. The slowdown should be negligible compared to everything else
    27→//! unless the number of forks gets absurdly high.
    28→//!
    29→//! Denormalizing the data structure further may improve performance if it turns out to be bad.
    30→//! Having [`Segment`] store a list of its children may help. The original design stored a list of
    31→//! children and the best leaf segment ID in each [`UnfinalizedBlock`] as well as the parent
    32→//! [`Location`] in each [`Segment`], but that turned out to be unnecessary.
    33→//!
    34→//! This implementation is inspired by [`proto_array`].
    35→//! Compared to [`proto_array`], this implementation has several advantages:
    36→//! - Block ancestors can be looked up using binary search or interpolation search
    37→//!   (as long as the number of forks is small, that is).
    38→//! - Fewer fields are needed in each unfinalized block.
    39→//! - It's easy to determine the number of forks.
    40→//!
    41→//! Block and attestation processing is split into pairs of `validate_*` and `apply_*` methods.
    42→//! The `validate_*` methods do not mutate [`Store`] and can be used to process objects in parallel.
    43→//! Because of the split some functions from the Fork Choice specification do not have exact
    44→//! equivalents in the implementation.
    45→//!
    46→//! This implementation makes use of persistent data structures, but they are not required for the
    47→//! algorithm to work. They're only used to make snapshots cheap.
    48→//!
    49→//! This implementation prunes orphans as soon as possible. As a result, some validations for both
    50→//! blocks and attestations are implicit. Also, this implementation discards blocks and attestations
    51→//! that could be used for slashing. However, transitively delayed objects are not pruned.
    52→//!
    53→//! This implementation performs some of the validations listed in the Networking specifications,
